chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. Folding paper finds lines of symmetry, turning cut-outs finds angles of symmetry, and each idea is tested on rangoli, kolam, wheels and tiles from everyday life.

points.title: Fold it, turn it, then say it
points.text: Every new idea starts from a paper fold or a paper turn, so a line of symmetry and an angle of symmetry are first seen, then named.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the figure is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: Lines and turns are different
points.text: A figure may have lines, turns, both or neither, and the plan keeps the two ideas apart until the chapter brings them together.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'the diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a fold or a cut-out, never just a rule.

design_references.text: maths6_ch7 new_design Phase 2 plan: framing intro with one hook, idea topics ending in one doer, optional tool where the manipulation is the idea, a practice topic after each idea topic with one video per book question, one summary topic.

modules.module_summary: A line of symmetry cuts a figure into mirror halves that overlap when folded. Figures can have one line, many lines or none, and folding, punching and cutting paper make symmetric shapes.

concepts.concept_name: Which pictures repeat a pattern?

content.text:
Look around you, you may find many objects that catch your attention. Some such things are shown below: [Flower, Butterfly, Rangoli, Pinwheel]
There is something beautiful about the pictures above.
The flower looks the same from many different angles. What about the butterfly? No doubt, the colours are very attractive. But what else about the butterfly appeals to you?
On the other hand, look at this picture of clouds. There is no such repetitive pattern.
We can say that the first four figures are symmetrical and the last one is not symmetrical. A symmetry refers to a part or parts of a figure that are repeated in some definite pattern.

concepts.concept_name: Mirror halves: the fold test

content.text:
Figure (a) shows the picture of a blue triangle with a dotted line. What if you fold the triangle along the dotted line? Yes, one half of the triangle covers the other half completely. These are called mirror halves!
What about Figure (b) with the four puzzle pieces and a dotted line passing through the middle? Are they mirror halves? No, when we fold along the line, the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

content.text:
Worked example: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?
1. Fold the triangle along the dotted line: the halves match exactly.
2. Fold the puzzle pieces along their dotted line: the bumps and holes on the two sides do not match.
3. Only an exact match gives mirror halves.
Answer: For the triangle: yes, one half covers the other exactly, so they are mirror halves. For the puzzle pieces: no, when folded along the line the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

A line that cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along that line is called a line of symmetry of the figure.
What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? [Taj Mahal, Gopuram]

content.text:
Worked example: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
1. Imagine a vertical line down the middle of each building.
2. Check that the left side matches the right side.
3. Clouds have no repeating pattern, so no symmetry.
Answer: Each of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram has a vertical line down the middle with the left half matching the right half, and many parts repeat in a pattern (towers, windows, tiers). The clouds have no repeating pattern, so they are not symmetrical.

tool_config.title: Fold and Find Lines
tool_config.idea: A line is a line of symmetry only if folding along it makes the two parts overlap exactly.
tool_config.screen: A figure on a sheet; a draggable fold line that can be set vertical, horizontal or at an angle; a Fold button that flips one side over the line with a ghost of the other side; an overlap meter; a list of lines found so far.
student_does: Predict whether the fold will work before pressing Fold.
Drag the fold line to a position and press Fold.
Keep the lines that overlap and count them, or say none.
challenges: An isosceles triangle (1 line).
A square (4 lines).
A rectangle that is not a square (2 lines, and the diagonal fails).
A kite (1 line).
A scalene triangle (0 lines).
A regular hexagon (6 lines).
feedback: A fold that leaves a corner sticking out shows the unmatched part in red, so equal-looking halves are seen not to overlap.
A wrong count shows the lines found so far on the figure and asks to try another direction.
A solved card shows each line of symmetry as a dashed line with the two halves overlapping.
tool_config.done_when: All six figures have the right number of lines.

hint_ladder.text: What does it mean for two halves to overlap exactly?
Try a vertical, a horizontal and a slanted fold on the figure.
Press Fold on a line and look for any part that sticks out.
The lines that overlap are shown as dashed lines; count them and a similar figure follows.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, first block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, first block): Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?
1. Try folding each picture along different lines.
2. Count the lines where the two halves match exactly: flower 6, rangoli 4, butterfly 1.
3. The pinwheel looks symmetric but its halves do not match when folded, and the cloud has no pattern.
Answer: Yes: the flower has 6 lines of symmetry, the rangoli has 4, and the butterfly has 1. The pinwheel and the cloud have no line of symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, first block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, first block): For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle. 1) Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch 2) Kite 3) Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles 4) L-shape 5) Scalene triangle
1. Fold each shape in your mind and look for a line that makes both halves match.
2. The kite folds along its vertical diagonal; the L-shape folds along the diagonal through its corner.
3. The slanted quadrilateral and the scalene triangle have no matching fold.
Answer: Shape 1 has one line of symmetry (a slanted line through its tip). Shape 2 (kite) has one vertical line of symmetry. Shape 3 has none. Shape 4 (L-shape) has one diagonal line of symmetry through its corner. Shape 5 (scalene triangle) has none.

concepts.concept_name: Folding a square four ways

content.text:
Does a square have only one line of symmetry?
Take a square piece of paper. By folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
Here are the different folds giving different lines of symmetry.
Fold the paper into half vertically.
Fold it again into half horizontally (i.e., you have folded it twice). Now open out the folds.
Again fold the square into half (for a third time now), but this time along a diagonal, as shown in the figure. Again, open it.
Fold it into half (for the fourth time), but this time along the other diagonal, as shown in the figure. Open out the fold.
Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

content.text:
1. Predict first: does a square have only one line of symmetry? How many folds do you think work?
2. Fold it in half vertically, then horizontally: two lines of symmetry.
3. Fold along one diagonal and then the other: two more lines, in all 4.
4. No other fold makes the two halves overlap, so the square has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
1. Fold the square in half vertically, then horizontally.
2. Fold it along one diagonal, then along the other diagonal.
3. Each fold makes the two halves overlap exactly, so there are 4 lines.
Answer: No. A square has 4 lines of symmetry: a vertical fold, a horizontal fold, and the two diagonals.

content.text:
Worked example: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?
1. The four folds are the vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals.
2. No other fold line makes the halves overlap.
3. So the count is 4.
Answer: No, there is no other way to fold the square. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Finding all the lines of a figure

content.text: Thus, figures can have multiple lines of symmetry. The figures below also have multiple lines of symmetry. Can you find them all?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a snowflake-like ring, a twisted six-petal flower and a four-loop design. Which has the most lines, and which has none?
2. Try vertical, horizontal and slanted folds on each design, and count the folds where the halves overlap.
3. The ring has 6 lines and the four-loop design has 4 lines. The twisted flower matches no mirror image, so it has no line of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.
1. Fold each figure in your mind along vertical, horizontal and slanted lines.
2. Count the lines where both halves match.
3. The twisted petal flower never matches its mirror image, so no line.
Answer: Figure 1: 6 lines. Figure 2: no line of symmetry (it only has rotational symmetry). Figure 3: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals).

concepts.concept_name: Is the diagonal of a rectangle a line of symmetry?

content.text:
We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Let us take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry?
First, see the rectangle and answer this question. Then, take a rectangular piece of paper and check if the two parts overlap by folding it along its diagonal. What do you observe?

content.text:
1. Predict first: the diagonal of a square is a line of symmetry. Is the diagonal of a long rectangle one too?
2. Fold the rectangle along its diagonal: the two triangles are equal in size, but one corner sticks out past the other.
3. Equal halves are not enough. The halves must overlap exactly, so a rectangle that is not a square has only 2 lines of symmetry, the vertical and the horizontal.

content.text:
Worked example: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.
1. Cut a rectangle that is longer than it is wide.
2. Fold along a diagonal.
3. The corners and sides do not meet, so the halves do not overlap.
Answer: No. The diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry: when folded along the diagonal the two parts do not overlap.

Try vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds on every figure.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines, a square 4 and a regular hexagon 6.
A triangle can have 0, 1 or 3 lines of symmetry, never exactly 2.

maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A diagonal is a line joining two opposite corners.
Folding a rectangle that is longer than it is wide along its diagonal: the two corners off the diagonal do not meet, and the long side lands on the short side.
A long side cannot cover a short side, so the two parts do not overlap.
The matching folds of a rectangle are straight down and straight across, not the diagonals.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) a square drawn tilted like a diamond, and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles. a) square drawn like a diamond; eight-pointed star b) triangle with equal sides and equal angles c) hexagon with equal sides and equal angles
1. For a regular shape, the number of lines equals the number of sides.
2. A square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3 and a regular hexagon 6.
3. The eight-pointed star has 8 lines through its points and notches.
Answer: (a) tilted square: 4; eight-pointed star: 8. (b) equilateral triangle: 3. (c) regular hexagon: 6.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Trace each figure and draw the lines of symmetry, if any. There are eight figures: four rhombus-pattern figures (1: one rhombus sitting on top of two rhombi that touch each other; 2: three rhombi in a row joined at their left-right corners; 3: a large diamond made of four small rhombi; 4: four rhombi in two columns of two, overlapping, standing in an X-like arrangement) and four figures on squared grids (5: a square inside a bigger square with the inner square divided into four; 6: an octagon-like shape with long vertical sides; 7: a five-sided shape like a kite with a flat right side; 8: a four-pointed star). 1) rhombus pattern 1 (one rhombus above two) 2) three rhombi in a row 3) large diamond of four rhombi 4) four overlapping rhombi, two columns 5) square inside a square on grid 6) octagon-like shape on grid 7) five-sided shape on grid 8) four-pointed star on grid
1. Trace the figure on paper or imagine folding it.
2. Try vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds.
3. Count the folds where the two halves overlap.
Answer: 1: 1 line (vertical). 2: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 3: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 4: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 5: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals). 6: 2 lines (vertical and horizontal). 7: 1 line (horizontal). 8: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and two diagonals).

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Find the lines of symmetry for the kolam below. The kolam is a large six-sided (hexagonal) pattern made of dots and star shapes made of rhombi, with the same design repeating around the centre.
1. Look for lines through the centre where one side matches the other.
2. The pattern repeats 6 times around the centre, so there are 6 lines.
Answer: The kolam has 6 lines of symmetry: one vertical line, one horizontal line and four slanted lines, all through the centre.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry? a) triangle with exactly one line of symmetry b) triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry c) triangle with no line of symmetry d) Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?
1. Two equal sides give one line: the line from the apex to the middle of the base.
2. All three sides equal give three lines.
3. If a triangle has two lines of symmetry it is forced to have all three, so exactly two cannot happen.
Answer: (a) An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). (b) An equilateral triangle. (c) A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry. a) exactly one line of symmetry, with a curved boundary b) exactly two lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary c) exactly four lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
1. Start with a symmetric shape such as a square or an arrow shape.
2. Replace some edges by curves, placing the same curve on each matching side.
3. Count the lines to check.
Answer: Any correct drawing works. Example: (a) a semicircle (one line, perpendicular to the straight edge) or a shape with a round top and a symmetrical body; (b) an ellipse or a rectangle with rounded bumps at the top and bottom (vertical and horizontal lines); (c) a circle-bump flower of four equal round loops around a square (4 lines).

final_answer.value: two equal sides: one line; all sides equal: three lines; all sides different: none; exactly two lines: not possible
final_answer.spoken: a triangle with two equal sides has one line, with all sides equal has three, and with all sides different has none, and exactly two is not possible

never_show: the verdict on exactly two lines before the answer beat
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides has exactly one line, from the corner where the equal sides meet to the middle of the third side.
A triangle with all three sides equal has three lines, one from each corner to the middle of the opposite side.
A triangle with all sides different has no line.
If a triangle had two lines, then two pairs of sides would be equal, which makes all three sides equal and gives three lines. So exactly two lines is not possible.
Check: count the folds again on each drawn triangle.

concepts.concept_name: Reflecting a square in its vertical line

content.text:
So far we have been saying that when we fold a figure along a line of symmetry, the two parts overlap completely. We could also say that the part of the figure on one side of the line of symmetry is reflected by the line to the other side; similarly, the part of the figure on the other side of the line of symmetry is reflected to the first side! Let us understand this by labeling some points on the figure.
The figure shows a square with its corners labeled A, B, C and D. Let us first consider the vertical line of symmetry. When we reflect the square along this line, the points B, C on the right get reflected to the left side and occupy the positions occupied earlier by A, D. What happens to the points A, D? A occupies the position occupied by B and D that of C!

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Copy the following on squared paper. Complete them so that the blue line is a line of symmetry. Problem (a) has been done for you. (b) A stepped red shape above a horizontal blue line, with a slanted edge ending at the right end of the line. (c) A staircase-shaped red outline next to a slanted (diagonal) blue line. (d) A small red shape touching a vertical blue line on a narrow grid. (e) A red five-sided outline hanging below a horizontal blue line. (f) A red outline with corner cuts next to a diagonal blue line. Hint: for (c) and (f), see if rotating the book helps! b) red stepped shape above a horizontal blue line c) staircase outline beside a diagonal blue line d) small shape on a vertical line e) five-sided red outline hanging below a horizontal line f) red outline with corner cuts beside a diagonal line
1. Pick a corner of the red outline and count its distance from the blue line.
2. Go the same distance on the other side and mark the mirror corner.
3. Join the mirror corners in the same order.
4. For a diagonal line, turn the page so that the line is vertical or horizontal.
Answer: In each case, reflect every point of the red outline in the blue line: draw each mirror point at the same distance on the other side, then join the mirror points. The finished shape is symmetric about the blue line. (b) the shape is mirrored below the horizontal line; (c) mirrored across the diagonal; (d) the left red part is mirrored to the right of the vertical line; (e) mirrored above the horizontal line; (f) mirrored across the diagonal.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left. a) diagonals, red bottom segment b) diagonals, red left zigzag c) vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline d) vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline e) vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag f) vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline
1. Reflect the given red part in one blue line.
2. Reflect the new figure (old plus new) in the other blue line.
3. Check that both blue lines now act as folds.
Answer: Reflect the red part in the first blue line, then reflect the whole result in the second blue line. Then the figure is symmetric about both. (a) completes to a square; (b) completes to a four-sided figure with an arrow-head point on each side; (c) a symmetric cross-like stepped shape; (d) a symmetric octagon-like shape; (e) a symmetric stepped cross shape with a notched top and bottom; (f) a symmetric butterfly-like shape.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q13 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q13 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Copy the following on a dot grid. For each figure draw two more lines to make a shape that has a line of symmetry. The six dot-grid figures each show a few connected line segments.
1. Look at the open figure and imagine a line that could be a mirror.
2. Mark the mirror image of each end of the open figure.
3. Join these to complete the two lines.
Answer: Any correct completion works. For each figure choose a mirror line (it can be vertical, horizontal or slanted), then draw the mirror images of the two end points to close the shape with two extra lines. The solutions show closed shapes (four-sided or five-sided) each with one drawn line of symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Ink Blot Devils

content.text:
So far we have seen symmetrical figures and asymmetrical figures. How does one generate such symmetrical figures? Let us explore this.
Ink Blot Devils
You enjoyed doing this earlier in Class 5. Take a piece of paper. Fold it in half. Open the paper and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half.
Now press the halves together and then open the paper again.
What do you see?
Is the resulting figure symmetric?
If yes, where is the line of symmetry?
Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts?
Try making more such patterns.

3. A random blot usually has no other line of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.
1. Fold the paper in half and put ink on one half.
2. Press the halves together and open: the ink prints a mirror image on the other half.
3. The crease is the line of symmetry.
Answer: You see a blot pattern with the same shape on both sides of the crease. Yes, it is symmetric and the fold (crease) is the line of symmetry. Usually no other line works, since the shape is random, so there is just one line of symmetry.

Worked example: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is made along the dotted line shown (the dotted line forms a notch shape starting at the fold). Draw a sketch of how the paper will look when unfolded. Do you see a line of symmetry in this figure? What is it?

concepts.concept_name: Intricate paper cut-outs

content.text:
There are more ways of folding and cutting pieces of paper to get symmetric shapes.
Use thin rectangular coloured paper. Fold it several times and create some intricate patterns by cutting the paper, like the one shown here. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design. Use such decorative paper cut-outs for festive occasions.

1. Predict first: if you fold a strip three times and cut once, how many copies of the cut appear?
2. Each fold doubles the copies: one fold gives 2, two folds give 4, three folds give 8.
3. Every fold line becomes a line of symmetry of the opened design.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded? a) two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height b) two holes close together near the top right corner c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other d) four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)
1. The fold line is the line of symmetry, halfway between each pair of matching holes and at right angles to the line joining them.
2. For (d), four holes means two lines of symmetry: fold in half, then in half again.
Answer: (a) a vertical fold through the middle; (b) a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; (c) a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; (d) the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.

content.question: In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded? a) two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height b) two holes close together near the top right corner c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other d) four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)
steps: The fold line is the line of symmetry, halfway between each pair of matching holes and at right angles to the line joining them.
For (d), four holes means two lines of symmetry: fold in half, then in half again.
content.answer: (a) a vertical fold through the middle; (b) a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; (c) a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; (d) the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the other hole(s). Five shapes each show one hole and a dashed line of symmetry: (a) a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left; (b) a square with a horizontal middle line and a hole in the lower right; (c) an equilateral triangle with a vertical line through the apex and a hole just left of the line near the middle; (d) a circle with a slanted diameter and a hole above the line near the right; (e) a circle with a diagonal line from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left, close to the line. a) square, diagonal line, hole near top left b) square, horizontal middle line, hole lower right c) triangle, vertical line, hole left of the line d) circle, slanted diameter, hole above the line e) circle, diagonal line, hole near top left
1. Draw a line from the given hole that meets the dashed line at a right angle.
2. Go the same distance past the dashed line.
3. Mark the new hole there.
Answer: In every shape the other hole is the mirror image of the given hole in the dashed line: same distance from the line, on the opposite side. (a) the other hole is across the diagonal, near the top edge; (b) in the upper right, directly above the given hole; (c) to the right of the vertical line at the same height; (d) below the slanted line, mirrored; (e) on the other side of the diagonal, mirrored.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Here are some questions on paper cutting. Consider a vertical fold. We represent it by a picture of a sheet folded in half vertically with an arrow. Similarly, a horizontal fold is represented by a sheet folded in half horizontally with an arrow.
1. A vertical fold makes a vertical crease.
2. A horizontal fold makes a horizontal crease.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): After each of the following cuts, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened. After you have made your prediction, make the cutouts and verify your answer. (a) A green sheet is folded once; a wavy cut is made from the edge, along a dotted line, with a narrow pinched middle. (b) A green sheet is folded once; a cut shaped like a notched banner (with an arrow-head notch) is made. (c) A purple sheet is folded vertically and then horizontally (4 layers) and notches are cut at the corner and edge. (d) A yellow sheet is folded vertically once and rectangular notches are cut along the open edge. a) green sheet folded once, wavy cut near the open edge b) green sheet folded once, banner-shaped cut with an arrow-head notch c) purple sheet folded twice (vertical then horizontal), notches cut d) yellow sheet folded vertically, notches cut along the open edge
1. Picture opening the sheet.
2. The cut appears again on the other side of each fold, as a mirror image.
3. With two folds, the cut appears four times (once in each quarter).
Answer: In every case the opened paper shows the cut shape together with its mirror image in each fold line. (a) a bow-tie like shape with wavy sides, symmetric about the fold line; (b) a banner shape with an arrow-head notch at each end, symmetric about the fold line; (c) a sheet with notches at the edges/corners and small rectangular holes arranged symmetrically on both sides of the vertical and the horizontal fold; (d) a rectangle with notches on both the left and right edges and a square hole in the middle.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Suppose you have to get each of these shapes with some folds and a single straight cut. How will you do it? (a) The hole in the centre is a square (sides parallel to the sides of the sheet). (b) The hole in the centre is a square (tilted so that its corners point up, down, left and right). Note: for the above two questions, check if the 4-sided figures in the centre satisfy both the properties of a square. a) square hole in the centre with sides parallel to the paper b) tilted square hole in the centre
1. Fold twice so that the centre of the sheet is at one corner of the small folded square.
2. For (a) cut off a small square at that corner.
3. For (b) cut a slanting line across that corner, removing a triangle.
4. Open the sheet: the four mirror copies join to make the hole.
Answer: (a) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner (the corner that is the centre of the sheet) cut a small square with all sides closed, using straight cuts parallel to the folds. (b) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner cut along one slanting (diagonal) line so that a small triangle is removed; opening gives a tilted square.

names.Ruhee: activity: punch holes in folded paper to create symmetric patterns

never_show: a fold line drawn through a hole
maths_rules: A hole and its partner are mirror pictures, so the fold line is the line of symmetry between them
The fold line is halfway between the two holes and at a right angle to the line joining them
Two holes left and right at the same height: the line joining them is horizontal, so the fold is vertical, through the middle
Two holes close together near the top right corner: the fold is the diagonal from bottom left to top right, between the two holes
Two holes on the right edge, one above the other: the line joining them is vertical, so the fold is horizontal, through the middle
One fold gives 2 layers and 2 holes; 2 folds give 2 x 2 = 4 layers and 4 holes
Four holes from a single punch: fold vertically, then horizontally (or the other way round); the one hole goes through 4 layers
Check: folding the opened sheet along the line puts each hole on its partner

concepts.concept_name: The windmill and its centre of rotation

content.text:
The paper windmill in the picture looks symmetrical but there is no line of symmetry! However, if you fold it, the two halves will not exactly overlap. On the other hand, if you rotate it by 90° about the red point at the centre, the windmill looks exactly the same.
We say that the windmill has rotational symmetry.
When talking of rotational symmetry, there is always a fixed point about which the object is rotated. This fixed point is called the centre of rotation.
Will the windmill above look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
No!
An angle through which a figure can be rotated to look exactly the same is called an angle of rotational symmetry, or just an angle of symmetry, for short.
For the windmill, the angles of symmetry are 90° (quarter turn), 180° (half turn), 270° (three-quarter turn) and 360° (full turn). Observe that when any figure is rotated by 360°, it comes back to its original position, so 360° is always an angle of symmetry.
Thus, we see that the windmill has 4 angles of symmetry.
Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?

Will the windmill above look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
No!
An angle through which a figure can be rotated to look exactly the same is called an angle of rotational symmetry, or just an angle of symmetry, for short.
For the windmill, the angles of symmetry are 90° (quarter turn), 180° (half turn), 270° (three-quarter turn) and 360° (full turn). Observe that when any figure is rotated by 360°, it comes back to its original position, so 360° is always an angle of symmetry.
Thus, we see that the windmill has 4 angles of symmetry.
Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?

content.text:
Worked example: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
1. Rotate the square about its centre by a quarter turn: it overlaps itself.
2. Each further quarter turn does the same: 90°, 180°, 270°.
3. A full turn of 360° brings every corner back to its own place.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a Class 6 maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two shapes side by side with wide space between: the strip in its start position on the left, the half turned strip on the right over a dotted outline.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, first block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, first block): Find the angles of symmetry for the given figures about the point marked with a dot. (a) A plus shape made of a vertical rectangle and a horizontal rectangle of the same length crossing at their middles, dot at the centre. (b) A vertical line with a dot at its middle, and a small square on the right of the top end and another small square on the right of the bottom end. (c) A horizontal segment joining the middles of two long vertical lines (a sideways H), dot at the middle of the horizontal segment. a) Plus shape of two equal rectangles. b) Vertical line with a small square on the right of each end. c) Horizontal bar joining two vertical lines.
1. Rotate each figure about the dot and see after which turns it fits itself.
2. (a) a quarter turn fits, so 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
3. (b) a half turn puts the top square on the left side of the bottom, so it does not fit: only 360°. (c) a half turn fits: 180°, 360°.
Answer: a) 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. b) 360° only. c) 180°, 360°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, first block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, first block): Which of the following figures have more than one angle of symmetry? The seven figures are: a circle with a cross dividing it into 4 equal parts; a downward-pointing triangle with a dot inside; a circle divided into 3 equal parts by three spokes; a four-bladed pinwheel with a red cross; an X made of two crossing lines; a five-pointed star with a dot at its centre; a shape like the letter B made of a vertical line with two half circles on its right.
1. Test each figure by turning it about its centre.
2. The circle with 4 parts (order 4), circle with 3 parts (order 3), pinwheel (order 4), X (order 4) and star (order 5) all fit again before a full turn.
3. The triangle (as drawn) and the B-shape only fit after 360°.
Answer: Five figures: the circle with the cross (4 equal parts), the circle with 3 equal parts, the four-bladed pinwheel, the X, and the five-pointed star.

maths_rules: every figure fits after the full turn of 360 degrees, so a figure has more than one angle of symmetry only if a smaller turn also fits
circle with a cross, 4 equal parts: a 90 degree turn fits
circle with 3 spokes, 3 equal parts: a turn of 360 / 3 = 120 degrees fits
four bladed pinwheel: a 90 degree turn fits
X of two crossing lines: a half turn of 180 degrees fits, so it fits before 360 degrees
five pointed star with its centre dot: a turn of 360 / 5 = 72 degrees fits
downward triangle with a dot, as drawn, and the B shape (a vertical line with two half circles on its right): fit only after 360 degrees
slip: a fold line shows a mirror match, not a turn; the B shape has a fold line but no turn smaller than 360 degrees fits

concepts.concept_name: Four radial arms

content.text:
Consider this figure, a picture with 4 radial arms. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they? Note that the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°.
Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
To check if the figure drawn indeed has 4 angles of symmetry, you could draw the figure on two different pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one of the papers. Keep the figure on the paper fixed and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
1. The arms are equal and 90° apart.
2. Each quarter turn moves an arm onto the next arm.
3. So the turns 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° all work.
Answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.

concepts.concept_name: Four radial arms

content.text:
Worked example: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
1. For 4 angles of symmetry, a quarter turn must put each arm on the next arm.
2. So all four angles between neighbouring arms must be equal.
3. They must add to 360°, so each is 90°.
Answer: Not if the arms are identical and only the angles are changed: the 4 arms must stay equally spaced, with 90° between neighbours. Changing the angles gives fewer angles of symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Four radial arms

content.text:
Worked example: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
1. Draw the figure twice and cut out one copy.
2. Pin the cutout at the centre and turn it over the other copy.
3. Count the turns after which it fits exactly.
Answer: A correct check shows the cutout fits exactly onto the fixed figure at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only.

concepts.concept_name: Exactly two angles, and three unequal arms

content.text:
How will you modify the figure above so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
Here is one way:
We have seen figures having 4 and 2 angles of symmetry. Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
Let us try with 3 radial arms as in the figure below. How many angles of symmetry does it have and what are they?
Here is a figure with three radial arms.
Trace and cut out a copy of this figure. By rotating the cutout over this figure determine its angles of rotation.
We see that only a full turn or a rotation of 360° will bring the figure back into itself. So this figure does not have rotational symmetry as 360 degrees is its only angle of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
1. Change the figure so a quarter turn no longer fits.
2. Keep it the same after a half turn (180°).
3. Then the angles of symmetry are only 180° and 360°.
Answer: Make opposite arms alike but the two pairs different, for example the book's figure where the top arm bends to the right at its end and the bottom arm bends to the left (a half turn copy), with the left and right arms straight. Then only 180° and 360° work.

concepts.concept_name: Exactly two angles, and three unequal arms

content.text:
Worked example: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
1. 3 angles of symmetry means 3 turns that fit, including 360°.
2. 3 equal arms at equal gaps share the full turn equally.
3. Each gap is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
Answer: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart.

concepts.concept_name: Why three equal arms need 120°

content.text:
However, can anything in the figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry?
Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?
If a figure with three radial arms should have rotational symmetry, then a rotated version of it should overlap with the original. Here are rough diagrams of both of them.
If these two figures must overlap, what can you tell about the angles?
Observe that ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
So, ∠A = ∠B = ∠C. What must this angle be?
We know that a full turn has 360 degrees. This is equally distributed amongst these three angles. So each angle must be 360°/3 = 120°.
So, the radial arms figure with 3 arms shows rotational symmetry when the angle between adjacent dotted lines is 120°. Use paper cutouts to verify this observation.
Now how many angles of rotation does the figure have and what are they?
Note: The colours have been added to show the rotations.

2. Angle A must land on B, B on C and C on A, so the three angles are equal.
3. The full turn of 360° is shared equally, so each angle is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
4. The figure then turns onto itself at 120°, 240° and 360°.

concepts.concept_name: Why three equal arms need 120°

content.text:
Worked example: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?
1. After 120° each arm lands on the next arm.
2. After 240° (120° + 120°) it fits again.
3. After 360° (120° + 120° + 120°) it is back to the start.
Answer: 3 angles of symmetry: 120°, 240°, 360°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, first block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, first block): Give the order of rotational symmetry for each figure: (a) a slanted line with a small flag at its top left end and another small flag at its bottom right end, dot at its middle; (b) an X made of two crossing lines with an angle marked at the top; (c) a six-pointed star with a dot at the centre; (d) three bent arms with fists arranged around a centre; (e) a plus shape made of two rectangles with a dot at the centre; (f) a regular pentagon with a dot at the centre. a) Slanted line with flags at its two ends b) X of two crossing lines c) Six-pointed star d) Three bent arms with fists e) Plus shape f) Regular pentagon
1. Order of rotational symmetry means the number of angles of symmetry, counting 360°.
2. Count how many times the figure fits itself in one full turn.
3. (a) 180° and 360°: 2. (c) 6 points: 6. (d) 3 arms: 3. (f) 5 sides: 5.
Answer: a) 2, b) 4, c) 6, d) 3, e) 4, f) 5.

maths_rules: order of rotational symmetry = number of angles of symmetry = number of turns that fit in one full turn, counting 360°
the book's windmill fits at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°, so its order is 4
flagged slanted line: fits after 180° and 360°, order 2
two crossing lines at right angles: fits after 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°, order 4
six pointed star with equal points: 360 ÷ 6 = 60, order 6
three bent arms: 360 ÷ 3 = 120, order 3
plus shape with four equal arms: 360 ÷ 4 = 90, order 4
regular pentagon: 360 ÷ 5 = 72, order 5

open_questions: The crossing-lines figure is read as two lines crossing at a right angle (order 4, as the book answer says). If the marked angle at the top is not a right angle, its order would be 2.

Worked example: Look at the pinwheel picture (a blue figure made of many triangles arranged around a hexagon). Which pattern is repeating? Hint: look at the hexagon first. What figure repeats along each side of the hexagon, what is its shape, and how do these shapes move as you go along the boundary of the hexagon?
1. Find the hexagon in the middle.
2. See what is stuck to each side: the same blue shape made of triangles.
3. Going around the boundary, the shape repeats in the same turned position each time.
Answer: The same shape made of triangles is stuck to each side of the hexagon, and it repeats in the same way, one after another, as you go around the boundary of the hexagon.

concepts.concept_name: Five, six and seven arms

content.text:
Worked example: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What will be its smallest angle of symmetry? Is the number of degrees a whole number in this case? If not, express it as a mixed fraction.
1. 7 equal arms share the full turn of 360°.
2. 360 ÷ 7 gives 51 with remainder 3.
3. So the smallest angle is 51 3/7°, not a whole number.
Answer: 360 ÷ 7 is 51 3/7°. It is not a whole number.

concepts.concept_name: Angles are multiples of the smallest

content.text:
Let us list down the angles of symmetry for all the cases above.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
Do you observe something common about the angles of symmetries in these cases? The first set of numbers are all multiples of 180. The second are all multiples of 120. The third are all multiples of 90.
In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. You may wonder and ask if this will always happen. What do you think?
True or False
• Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry.
• If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

content.text:
Worked example: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°. Exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°. Exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. Will this always happen? What do you think?
1. Look at 120°, 240°, 360°: they are 1×, 2×, 3× of 120°.
2. Turning by the smallest angle twice is the same as turning by twice that angle.
3. So every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one.
Answer: Yes, the angles of symmetry are always multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. (2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360. 1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. 2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.
1. A full turn of 360° always brings any figure back to itself.
2. The smallest angle fits a whole number of times in 360°.
3. So a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of 360.
Answer: Both are True.

the angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle, so 360° is a multiple of the smallest angle

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, second block): Colour the sectors of the circle below so that the figure has i) 3 angles of symmetry, ii) 4 angles of symmetry, iii) what are the possible numbers of angles of symmetry you can obtain by colouring the sectors in different ways? The circle is divided into 12 equal sectors. i) 3 angles of symmetry ii) 4 angles of symmetry iii) Possible numbers of angles of symmetry
1. Each sector is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
2. 3 angles of symmetry need a pattern that repeats every 120°, that is every 4 sectors; 4 angles need a pattern repeating every 90°, every 3 sectors.
3. The pattern can repeat every 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 sectors, giving 12, 6, 4, 3, 2 or 1 angles of symmetry.
Answer: i) Colour every 4th sector (3 coloured sectors, 120° apart). ii) Colour every 3rd sector (4 coloured sectors, 90° apart). iii) The number of angles of symmetry can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 (at most 12).

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2, second block): In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?
1. Other angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.
2. 60 × 2 = 120°, 60 × 3 = 180°, 60 × 4 = 240°, 60 × 5 = 300°.
3. 60 × 6 = 360° (full turn).
Answer: 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.2, second block): In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
1. Angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.
2. Two angles less than 60° means the smallest angle d and 2d are below 60°, and 3d = 60°.
3. So d = 60 ÷ 3 = 20°.
Answer: 20°

content.text:
Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2, second block): Can we have a figure with rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: a. 45°? b. 17°? a) Smallest angle of symmetry 45° b) Smallest angle of symmetry 17°
1. The smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into 360°.
2. (a) 360 ÷ 45 = 8, so yes: 8 equal arms.
3. (b) 360 ÷ 17 is not a whole number (17 is not a factor of 360), so no.
Answer: a) Yes. b) No.

concepts.concept_name: A circle has no smallest angle

content.text:
Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures? It turns out that this is the case for most figures, except for the most symmetric shapes like the circle, whose symmetries we now discuss.
The circle is a fascinating figure. What happens when you rotate a circle clockwise about its centre? It coincides with itself. It does not matter what angle you rotate it by! So, for a circle, every angle is an angle of symmetry.

content.text:
1. Predict first: turn a circle about its centre by a tiny angle. Does it still match itself?
2. It does, whatever the angle, so every angle is an angle of symmetry.
3. Most figures have a smallest angle of symmetry. The circle does not.

content.text:
Worked example: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
1. A figure like a square has smallest angle 90°.
2. A circle fits itself after any turn.
3. So there is no smallest angle for a circle.
Answer: No. Most figures have one, but a circle does not: every angle is an angle of symmetry for a circle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: look at a bicycle wheel, a ceiling fan and a three-bladed propeller. Which turn onto themselves, and how many times in one full turn?
2. A fan with 3 equal blades matches itself 3 times in a full turn, a wheel with 8 equal spokes 8 times.

content.text:
Worked example: Like wheels, we can find other objects around us having rotational symmetry. Find them. (Shown: a three-bladed fan, a five-petal flower, a wheel with many spokes.)
1. Look around for objects with equal parts around a centre.
2. Check by imagining a turn about the centre.
3. Name the object and the smallest angle of symmetry.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.2, second block): How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does Ashoka Chakra have? (The Ashoka Chakra is a wheel with 24 equal spokes.)
1. The Chakra has 24 equal spokes around the centre.
2. Each angle between spokes is 360 ÷ 24 = 15°.
3. Angles: 15°, 30°, ... 360°, which is 24 angles; also 24 lines.
Answer: 24 lines of symmetry and 24 angles of symmetry.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a kite has a line of symmetry. Does it also turn onto itself at 180°?
2. No: a kite has one line and only the 360° turn. A twisted six-petal flower turns onto itself at 60° steps, but has no line.
3. So a figure with a line need not have turns, and a figure with turns need not have a line.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an equilateral triangle. How many lines of symmetry, and how many angles of symmetry?
2. 3 lines, and the angles 120°, 240° and 360°, so 3 angles.
3. A square has 4 lines and 4 angles. A regular figure with n equal sides has n lines and n angles of symmetry.
4. The equal counts are special to regular shapes. A kite has 1 line and 1 angle, and the twisted flower has 0 lines and 6 angles.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, second block): Draw two figures other than a circle and a square that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.
1. Choose a shape with equal parts around a centre.
2. Check that it can be folded to match itself.
3. Check that a turn less than 360° also fits.
Answer: Open ended. Examples: a plus sign of 4 equal arms (4 lines of symmetry, order 4), a four-petal flower (4 lines, order 4), an equilateral triangle (3 lines, order 3), a rectangle (2 lines, order 2).

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, second block): Draw, wherever possible, a rough sketch of: a. A triangle with at least two lines of symmetry and at least two angles of symmetry. b. A triangle with only one line of symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. c. A quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry. d. A quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. a) Triangle with at least two lines and two angles of symmetry b) Triangle with only one line of symmetry, no rotational symmetry c) Quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry d) Quadrilateral with reflection symmetry, no rotational symmetry
1. (a) Only an equilateral triangle has 2 or more lines.
2. (b) An isosceles triangle folds one way only and fits only after 360°.
3. (c) A slanted parallelogram fits after a half turn but cannot be folded. (d) An isosceles trapezium folds down the middle but a half turn does not fit.
Answer: a) Equilateral triangle: 3 lines, 3 angles (120°, 240°, 360°). b) Isosceles triangle (not equilateral): 1 line, no rotational symmetry. c) Parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus: no line, angles 180° and 360°. d) Isosceles trapezium: 1 line, no rotational symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2, second block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2, second block): This is a picture of the new Parliament Building in Delhi; its outer boundary is a triangle-like shape with its three corners cut off (3 long sides alternating with 3 short sides). a. Does the outer boundary of the picture have reflection symmetry? If so, draw the lines of symmetries. How many are they? b. Does it have rotational symmetry around its centre? If so, find the angles of rotational symmetry. a) Reflection symmetry? Number of lines b) Rotational symmetry? Angles
1. The outline is a hexagon with 3 long sides and 3 short sides alternating.
2. Each line through the middle of a long side and the middle of the opposite short side is a line of symmetry: 3 lines.
3. It fits after a third of a turn: 360 ÷ 3 = 120°, so 120°, 240°, 360°.
Answer: a) Yes, 3 lines of symmetry. b) Yes, 120°, 240°, 360°.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.2, second block): How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (The shapes are the regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon and decagon.)
1. A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry.
2. Triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10.
3. The sequence is the counting numbers from 3.
Answer: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: the counting numbers starting from 3.

1. A regular polygon with n sides fits itself after each turn of 360 ÷ n.
2. So it has n angles of symmetry, counting 360°.
3. Triangle 3, square 4, ... decagon 10: the counting numbers from 3.
Answer: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: the counting numbers starting from 3.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.2, second block): How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the last shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Koch Snowflake sequence, have? How many angles of symmetry? lines) Lines of symmetry for the 5 shapes angles) Angles of symmetry for the 5 shapes
1. The first shape is a triangle: 3 lines and 3 angles.
2. From the next shape on, the snowflake has 6 lines and 6 angles.
3. The later shapes keep the same symmetry: 6 and 6.
Answer: Lines of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6. Angles of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6.

final_answer.value: plus sign: 4 lines, 4 angles; triangle with 3 equal sides: 3 lines, 3 angles
final_answer.spoken: a plus sign with four equal arms has four lines and four angles of symmetry, and a triangle with three equal sides has three lines and three angles

never_show: a circle or a square as an answer
a leaning parallelogram accepted as having both kinds of symmetry
maths_rules: plus sign with 4 equal arms: fold lines are the vertical, the horizontal and the 2 slanting lines, so 4 lines of symmetry
360 / 4 = 90, so the plus sign fits after 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees: 4 angles of symmetry
triangle with 3 equal sides: one fold line from each corner to the middle of the opposite side, so 3 lines of symmetry
360 / 3 = 120, so the triangle fits after 120, 240 and 360 degrees: 3 angles of symmetry
the question excludes the circle and the square; neither answer is one of them
both shapes have a turn smaller than 360 degrees that fits, so both have rotational symmetry as well as reflection symmetry

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about drawing shapes that match themselves in two ways.

narration: <bookmark mark='line'/>A fold line where both halves cover each other exactly is called a line of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='angle'/>A turn that makes a shape look exactly the same is called an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='full'/>A full turn always fits, so three hundred sixty degrees is always an angle of symmetry. We need a smaller turn that fits too.

final_answer.value: triangle with three equal sides: 3 lines, 3 angles; triangle with two equal sides: 1 line, no rotational symmetry; leaning parallelogram: no line, angles 180 and 360; trapezium with equal slanting sides: 1 line, no rotational symmetry
final_answer.spoken: a triangle with three equal sides has three lines and three angles, a triangle with two equal sides has one line and no turn, a leaning parallelogram has no line but a half turn fits, and a four sided shape with equal slanting sides has one line and no turn

maths_rules: triangle with 3 equal sides: 3 fold lines, one from each corner to the middle of the opposite side
360 / 3 = 120, so it fits after 120, 240 and 360 degrees: 3 angles of symmetry
triangle with only 2 equal sides: 1 fold line, from the top corner to the middle of the third side; only 360 degrees fits, so no rotational symmetry
leaning parallelogram (no right angle, adjacent sides unequal): no fold line, neither the middle lines nor the diagonals; a half turn of 180 degrees fits, so its angles are 180 and 360

trapezium with one pair of parallel sides and equal slanting sides: 1 fold line through the middles of the parallel sides; a half turn does not fit because the parallel sides differ in length, so only 360 degrees fits
each of the four rules is met by its sketch, so all four can be drawn

3. Check for extra lines: if the tiles in the quarter slant one way, the diagonals fail and there are exactly 2 lines.

Worked example: Use the colour tiles given at the end of the book to complete the following figure so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry. 2. Reflect the top half across the horizontal red line into the bottom half.
3. Check that no other fold line works.

concepts.concept_name: A game won by a half turn

content.text:
Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses.
With what strategy can one play to win this game?

lines: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses.
With what strategy can one play to win this game?

content.text:
1. Predict first: two players cover two adjacent squares with a line in turn, and the player who cannot place a line loses. Who do you think wins?
2. The centre of the 6 by 6 grid is a corner point where 4 squares meet, so no line covers it.
3. After each move of the first player, the second player places a line on its 180° rotation about the centre. That place is free, so the second player always has a reply.
4. The first player runs out of moves first, so the second player wins.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses. With what strategy can one play to win this game?
1. The centre of the 6 by 6 grid is a corner point where 4 squares meet, so no line can cover it.
2. Every first-player move has a rotated copy that is free and does not overlap it.
3. So the second player always has a reply and the first player runs out of moves first.
Answer: The second player wins: after each move of the first player, place a line that is the 180° rotation about the centre of the grid of that move.

concepts.concept_name: Playing with Tiles b (section 9.2)

content.text:
Playing with Tiles b (section 9.2): Use 16 such colour tiles to make figures that have exactly: 1 line of symmetry; 2 lines of symmetry. 1) Figure with exactly 1 line of symmetry 2) Figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry
1. Lay 16 tiles in a 4 by 4 square.
2. For 1 line, make the left half a mirror image of the right half only.
3. For 2 lines, make it a mirror image both left to right and top to bottom, but not along the diagonals.
Answer: Open ended. A correct 4 by 4 arrangement has exactly one fold line (for example a vertical line) in the first case, and exactly two fold lines (for example vertical and horizontal) in the second.

concepts.concept_name: Playing with Tiles c (section 9.2)

content.text:
Playing with Tiles c (section 9.2): Use these colour tiles in making creative symmetric designs.
1. Pick a few tiles and arrange them around a centre.
2. Repeat or mirror them so the design matches itself.
3. Check by folding or turning.
Answer: Open ended. A correct design has at least one line of symmetry or rotational symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about symmetry

content.text:
When a figure is made up of parts that repeat in a definite pattern, we say that the figure has symmetry. We say that such a figure is symmetrical.
A line that cuts a plane figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along that line is called a line of symmetry or axis of symmetry of the figure.
A figure may have multiple lines of symmetry.
Sometimes a figure looks exactly the same when it is rotated by an angle about a fixed point. Such an angle is called an angle of symmetry of the figure. A figure that has an angle of symmetry strictly between 0 and 360 degrees is said to have rotational symmetry. The point of the figure about which the rotation occurs is called the centre of rotation.
A figure may have multiple angles of symmetry.
Some figures may have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry, while others may have angles of symmetry but no lines of symmetry. Some figures may have both lines of symmetry as well as angles of symmetry.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: a flower, a rangoli and a pinwheel repeat a part in a pattern, and the pattern is a line of symmetry, an angle of symmetry, or both.
2. A line of symmetry is tested by a fold, an angle of symmetry by a turn about a fixed centre.
3. Still open for you: how many lines and how many turns does a figure of your own design have?
