learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate the meaning of a line of symmetry, an angle of symmetry and the centre of rotation, and say which figures have lines, turns, both or neither.

objectives.objective_text: Students fold a figure along a dotted line, decide whether the two halves overlap exactly, and call such halves mirror halves.
Students define a line of symmetry as a line that cuts a figure into two parts that overlap exactly when folded, and name the vertical line of symmetry of a building.
Students fold a figure on the tool along a chosen line, check whether the halves overlap, and list the lines of symmetry the figure has, including none.
Students fold a square vertically, horizontally and along both diagonals, and conclude that a square has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.
Students list all the lines of symmetry of a design by trying every direction, and say when a design has no line at all.
Students test the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square by folding, and explain why the two triangles do not overlap.
Students count the lines of symmetry of squares, stars, regular shapes and kolam patterns, and draw triangles and curved figures with a given number of lines.
Students state where corners A, B, C and D of a square go when it is reflected in the vertical line of symmetry.
Students find where the corners of a square go for a reflection in a diagonal and in the horizontal line, and say which corners stay fixed.
Students reflect each point of a half-figure in a given mirror line and complete the figure so that the line, or both lines, are lines of symmetry.
Students make an ink blot on one half of a folded sheet and name the crease as the line of symmetry of the pattern.
Students predict the opened shape after a cut on a folded sheet, and identify the fold as the line of symmetry of the opened shape.
Students fold a strip several times, cut a pattern, and find the lines of symmetry of the repeating design.
Students punch or cut a folded sheet on the tool, unfold it, and find the fold lines that match a given pattern of holes or a given opened shape.
Students explain that a windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same after a 90° turn about its centre, and define the centre of rotation and an angle of symmetry.
Students list the angles of symmetry of a square and mark its centre of rotation at the crossing of the diagonals.
Students show by turning that a strip with one short side does not match itself after 180°, so its only angle of symmetry is 360°.
Students turn a figure about its marked centre on the tool, note each turn at which it matches itself, and list the angles of symmetry.
Students list the 4 angles of symmetry of a figure with 4 equal arms 90° apart, and check by turning a cut-out copy.
Students change a 4-arm figure to have only 2 angles of symmetry, and show that 3 arms with unequal angles give only 360°.
Students show that three arms give 3 angles of symmetry only when each angle between arms is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°, and list the angles 120°, 240° and 360°.
Students set the number of arms and the angles between them on the tool, turn the figure, and give its angles of symmetry and its order.
Students find the smallest angle of symmetry of figures with 5, 6 and 7 equal arms as 360 ÷ n, and write it as a mixed fraction when it is not whole.
Students explain that the angles of symmetry of a figure are the multiples of its smallest angle and that 360° is always one of them.
Students pick the number of equal turns on the tool, read the smallest angle 360 ÷ n and the ladder of its multiples, and decide whether a given smallest angle is possible.
Students explain that a circle looks the same after a turn of any angle, so it has no smallest angle of symmetry.
Students show that every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry, so the circle has endless lines of symmetry.
Students name everyday objects that look the same after a turn, such as wheels and fan blades, and give how many turns each has.
Students count the lines of symmetry and the angles of symmetry of a wheel with equal spokes such as the Ashoka Chakra.
Students give an example of a figure with a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry, and one with rotational symmetry but no line, and explain why one does not imply the other.
Students count the lines and the angles of symmetry of a square and an equilateral triangle, and see that a regular figure with n sides has n of each.
Students sort figures on the tool by lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry, and sketch figures that have a stated mix of the two.
Students complete a tile figure by reflecting the filled quarter so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.
Students explain why the second player always wins the 6 by 6 line-placing game by answering each move with its 180° rotation about the centre of the grid.
Students lay colour tiles on a 4 by 4 grid on the tool, and make designs with exactly 1 line, exactly 2 lines, or a turn of symmetry.
Students restate the meaning of a line of symmetry, an angle of symmetry and the centre of rotation, and say which figures have lines, turns, both or neither.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?

Book item: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
Book item: Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?

Book item: For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle. 1) Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch 2) Kite 3) Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles 4) L-shape 5) Scalene triangle
Book item: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
Book item: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

Book item: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.

Book item: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) a square drawn tilted like a diamond, and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles. a) square drawn like a diamond; eight-pointed star b) triangle with equal sides and equal angles c) hexagon with equal sides and equal angles

Book item: Trace each figure and draw the lines of symmetry, if any. There are eight figures: four rhombus-pattern figures (1: one rhombus sitting on top of two rhombi that touch each other; 2: three rhombi in a row joined at their left-right corners; 3: a large diamond made of four small rhombi; 4: four rhombi in two columns of two, overlapping, standing in an X-like arrangement) and four figures on squared grids (5: a square inside a bigger square with the inner square divided into four; 6: an octagon-like shape with long vertical sides; 7: a five-sided shape like a kite with a flat right side; 8: a four-pointed star). 1) rhombus pattern 1 (one rhombus above two) 2) three rhombi in a row 3) large diamond of four rhombi 4) four overlapping rhombi, two columns 5) square inside a square on grid 6) octagon-like shape on grid 7) five-sided shape on grid 8) four-pointed star on grid

Book item: Find the lines of symmetry for the kolam below. The kolam is a large six-sided (hexagonal) pattern made of dots and star shapes made of rhombi, with the same design repeating around the centre.

Book item: Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry? a) triangle with exactly one line of symmetry b) triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry c) triangle with no line of symmetry d) Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

Book item: Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry. a) exactly one line of symmetry, with a curved boundary b) exactly two lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary c) exactly four lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
Book item: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). When the square is reflected along the vertical line of symmetry, where do A, B, C and D go?

Book item: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left): what if we reflect along the diagonal from A to C? Where do points A, B, C and D go? What if we reflect along the horizontal line of symmetry?

Book item: Copy the following on squared paper. Complete them so that the blue line is a line of symmetry. Problem (a) has been done for you. (b) A stepped red shape above a horizontal blue line, with a slanted edge ending at the right end of the line. (c) A staircase-shaped red outline next to a slanted (diagonal) blue line. (d) A small red shape touching a vertical blue line on a narrow grid. (e) A red five-sided outline hanging below a horizontal blue line. (f) A red outline with corner cuts next to a diagonal blue line. Hint: for (c) and (f), see if rotating the book helps! b) red stepped shape above a horizontal blue line c) staircase outline beside a diagonal blue line d) small shape on a vertical line e) five-sided red outline hanging below a horizontal line f) red outline with corner cuts beside a diagonal line

Book item: Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left. a) diagonals, red bottom segment b) diagonals, red left zigzag c) vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline d) vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline e) vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag f) vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline
Book item: Copy the following on a dot grid. For each figure draw two more lines to make a shape that has a line of symmetry. The six dot-grid figures each show a few connected line segments.

Book item: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.

Book item: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is made along the dotted line shown (the dotted line forms a notch shape starting at the fold). Draw a sketch of how the paper will look when unfolded. Do you see a line of symmetry in this figure? What is it?

Book item: Make different symmetric shapes by folding and cutting. Use thin rectangular coloured paper, fold it several times and cut out intricate patterns, like the blue star-shaped cut-outs shown. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design.

Book item: In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded? a) two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height b) two holes close together near the top right corner c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other d) four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)

Book item: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the other hole(s). Five shapes each show one hole and a dashed line of symmetry: (a) a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left; (b) a square with a horizontal middle line and a hole in the lower right; (c) an equilateral triangle with a vertical line through the apex and a hole just left of the line near the middle; (d) a circle with a slanted diameter and a hole above the line near the right; (e) a circle with a diagonal line from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left, close to the line. a) square, diagonal line, hole near top left b) square, horizontal middle line, hole lower right c) triangle, vertical line, hole left of the line d) circle, slanted diameter, hole above the line e) circle, diagonal line, hole near top left

Book item: Here are some questions on paper cutting. Consider a vertical fold. We represent it by a picture of a sheet folded in half vertically with an arrow. Similarly, a horizontal fold is represented by a sheet folded in half horizontally with an arrow.

Book item: After each of the following cuts, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened. After you have made your prediction, make the cutouts and verify your answer. (a) A green sheet is folded once; a wavy cut is made from the edge, along a dotted line, with a narrow pinched middle. (b) A green sheet is folded once; a cut shaped like a notched banner (with an arrow-head notch) is made. (c) A purple sheet is folded vertically and then horizontally (4 layers) and notches are cut at the corner and edge. (d) A yellow sheet is folded vertically once and rectangular notches are cut along the open edge. a) green sheet folded once, wavy cut near the open edge b) green sheet folded once, banner-shaped cut with an arrow-head notch c) purple sheet folded twice (vertical then horizontal), notches cut d) yellow sheet folded vertically, notches cut along the open edge

Book item: Suppose you have to get each of these shapes with some folds and a single straight cut. How will you do it? (a) The hole in the centre is a square (sides parallel to the sides of the sheet). (b) The hole in the centre is a square (tilted so that its corners point up, down, left and right). Note: for the above two questions, check if the 4-sided figures in the centre satisfy both the properties of a square. a) square hole in the centre with sides parallel to the paper b) tilted square hole in the centre

Book item: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it). Can you see what repeats in it? What happens to the red petals when the rangoli is rotated by 90° around the centre?

Book item: A paper windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same when turned by 90° about the red point at its centre. Will the windmill look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
Book item: The windmill has exactly 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?
Book item: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
Book item: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
Book item: What are the other angles of symmetry of a square (besides 90°)?

Book item: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip. The strip is a trapezium shape (the top side is shorter than the bottom side, the two slanting sides are equal) with a dot marking its centre.
Book item: After the strip is rotated by 180° about its centre, does it overlap with the original strip? Why?

Book item: Find the angles of symmetry for the given figures about the point marked with a dot. (a) A plus shape made of a vertical rectangle and a horizontal rectangle of the same length crossing at their middles, dot at the centre. (b) A vertical line with a dot at its middle, and a small square on the right of the top end and another small square on the right of the bottom end. (c) A horizontal segment joining the middles of two long vertical lines (a sideways H), dot at the middle of the horizontal segment. a) Plus shape of two equal rectangles. b) Vertical line with a small square on the right of each end. c) Horizontal bar joining two vertical lines.

Book item: Which of the following figures have more than one angle of symmetry? The seven figures are: a circle with a cross dividing it into 4 equal parts; a downward-pointing triangle with a dot inside; a circle divided into 3 equal parts by three spokes; a four-bladed pinwheel with a red cross; an X made of two crossing lines; a five-pointed star with a dot at its centre; a shape like the letter B made of a vertical line with two half circles on its right.
Book item: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
Book item: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.

Book item: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
Book item: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
Book item: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
Book item: A figure has 3 radial arms but the angles between the arms are not equal. How many angles of symmetry does it have and what are they?
Book item: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry? Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?

Book item: If a figure with three radial arms has rotational symmetry, a rotated copy must overlap the original. What can you tell about the angles ∠A, ∠B and ∠C between the arms? What must this angle be?
Book item: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?

Book item: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each figure: (a) a slanted line with a small flag at its top left end and another small flag at its bottom right end, dot at its middle; (b) an X made of two crossing lines with an angle marked at the top; (c) a six-pointed star with a dot at the centre; (d) three bent arms with fists arranged around a centre; (e) a plus shape made of two rectangles with a dot at the centre; (f) a regular pentagon with a dot at the centre. a) Slanted line with flags at its two ends b) X of two crossing lines c) Six-pointed star d) Three bent arms with fists e) Plus shape f) Regular pentagon

Book item: Look at the pinwheel picture (a blue figure made of many triangles arranged around a hexagon). Which pattern is repeating? Hint: look at the hexagon first. What figure repeats along each side of the hexagon, what is its shape, and how do these shapes move as you go along the boundary of the hexagon?

Book item: Can you draw a figure with radial arms that has a) exactly 5 angles of symmetry, b) 6 angles of symmetry? Also find the angles of symmetry in each case. Hint: Use 5 radial arms for the first case. What should the angle between two adjacent radial arms be? a) Figure with radial arms having exactly 5 angles of symmetry; list the angles. b) Figure with radial arms having 6 angles of symmetry; list the angles.

Book item: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What will be its smallest angle of symmetry? Is the number of degrees a whole number in this case? If not, express it as a mixed fraction.

Book item: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°. Exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°. Exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. Will this always happen? What do you think?

Book item: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. (2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360. 1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. 2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

Book item: Colour the sectors of the circle below so that the figure has i) 3 angles of symmetry, ii) 4 angles of symmetry, iii) what are the possible numbers of angles of symmetry you can obtain by colouring the sectors in different ways? The circle is divided into 12 equal sectors. i) 3 angles of symmetry ii) 4 angles of symmetry iii) Possible numbers of angles of symmetry
Book item: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?
Book item: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
Book item: Can we have a figure with rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: a. 45°? b. 17°? a) Smallest angle of symmetry 45° b) Smallest angle of symmetry 17°
Book item: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
Book item: Take a point on the rim of a circle and join it to the centre. Extend the segment to a diameter. Is that diameter a line of reflection symmetry?
Book item: Like wheels, we can find other objects around us having rotational symmetry. Find them. (Shown: a three-bladed fan, a five-petal flower, a wheel with many spokes.)
Book item: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does Ashoka Chakra have? (The Ashoka Chakra is a wheel with 24 equal spokes.)
Book item: Draw two figures other than a circle and a square that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

Book item: Draw, wherever possible, a rough sketch of: a. A triangle with at least two lines of symmetry and at least two angles of symmetry. b. A triangle with only one line of symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. c. A quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry. d. A quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. a) Triangle with at least two lines and two angles of symmetry b) Triangle with only one line of symmetry, no rotational symmetry c) Quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry d) Quadrilateral with reflection symmetry, no rotational symmetry

Book item: This is a picture of the new Parliament Building in Delhi; its outer boundary is a triangle-like shape with its three corners cut off (3 long sides alternating with 3 short sides). a. Does the outer boundary of the picture have reflection symmetry? If so, draw the lines of symmetries. How many are they? b. Does it have rotational symmetry around its centre? If so, find the angles of rotational symmetry. a) Reflection symmetry? Number of lines b) Rotational symmetry? Angles

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (The shapes are the regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon and decagon.)

Book item: How many angles of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (Regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon.)

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the last shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Koch Snowflake sequence, have? How many angles of symmetry? lines) Lines of symmetry for the 5 shapes angles) Angles of symmetry for the 5 shapes

Book item: Use the colour tiles given at the end of the book to complete the following figure so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry. (An 8 by 8 grid of square tiles, each divided by a diagonal into a blue and a yellow triangle. The top left 4 by 4 quarter is already filled. A red vertical line and a red horizontal line pass through the middle of the grid.)

Book item: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses. With what strategy can one play to win this game?
Book item: Use 16 such colour tiles to make figures that have exactly: 1 line of symmetry; 2 lines of symmetry. 1) Figure with exactly 1 line of symmetry 2) Figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry
Book item: Use these colour tiles in making creative symmetric designs.
